lessons.title: Generics and Interfaces
lessons.explanation:
# 14 · Generics and Interfaces

The system-design block taught you what to build. This block is about
building it so that it is easy to keep changing. The first tool is the
type system. Generics let you write a cache, a repository or a pipeline
once and have the compiler check every use of it: a
`Repository<Customer, Long>` cannot be handed a `String` id, and a
`Key<Integer>` hands back an `Integer` with no cast. Interfaces with
default and static methods let you ship behaviour along with the
contract, the way `Comparator.thenComparing` and `Function.andThen` do.
Most "generics are hard" moments come from four ideas: bounds,
wildcards, inference and erasure. This module drills each one on code
shaped like what you write at work.

## The mental model

### 1 · A type parameter is a promise checked at compile time

```java
static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> items)
```

Read it right to left. `items` produces Ts (or subtypes). T must be
comparable with *something at or above it*, which is why `Beta extends
Version` works even though Beta is a `Comparable<Version>`, not a
`Comparable<Beta>`. This is the exact signature of `Collections.max`.
A **generic method** declares its own `<T>` before the return type, and
each call binds it again. A **generic class** binds it once per instance:
`new InMemoryRepository<Customer, Long>()`.

### 2 · PECS: producer extends, consumer super

```java
static <T> int copyAll(Collection<? super T> dst, Collection<? extends T> src)
```

| you only... | declare it as | example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| read Ts out of it | `? extends T` | `sum(Collection<? extends Number>)` |
| write Ts into it | `? super T` | `addRange(List<? super Integer>, ...)` |
| both read and write | plain `T` | `swap(List<T>)` |
| neither (size, clear) | `?` | `swapEnds(List<?>)` + a capture helper |

A `List<Integer>` is **not** a `List<Number>`. If it were, you could add
a `Double` to a list of Integers through the `List<Number>` view.
Wildcards are how you say "a list of some subtype, read-only for me".

### 3 · Interfaces carry behaviour

```java
interface PricingRule {
    BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal price);                  // the contract
    static PricingRule percentOff(int p) { ... }         // a factory
    default PricingRule andThen(PricingRule next) {      // a combinator
        return price -> next.apply(apply(price));
    }
}
```

A single abstract method makes it a functional interface, so lambdas
implement it. Default methods compose instances into new instances, and
static methods name the common cases. `Comparator` is the model citizen:
`comparing(...).thenComparing(..., reverseOrder())` reads like the
sentence it implements.

### 4 · Erasure: generics vanish at runtime

`List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class at runtime. So you
cannot write `new T[]`, `instanceof List<String>` or `T.class`, and a
raw type can smuggle a wrong value past the compiler with only a
warning. When you need the type at runtime, carry it yourself: a
`Class<T>` **type token** (`Key.of("port", Integer.class)`) can
`cast(...)` and check a value.

```
compile time:  Key<Integer> port   ctx.put(port, "x")   ✘ does not compile
runtime:       Key raw = port;     ctx.put(raw, "x")    only type.cast(...) stops it
```

## The details that bite

1. **`T extends Comparable<T>` is too strict.** It rejects subclasses
   that inherit `compareTo`. Use `Comparable<? super T>` (exercise 01).
2. **`>=` versus `>` changes which tie wins.** "First of equal maxima"
   needs a strict comparison (exercise 01).
3. **Return what the collection accepted, not what you offered.**
   `Set.add` returns false on a duplicate (exercise 02).
4. **You cannot write into a `List<?>`.** Capture the wildcard in a
   private `<T>` helper. Never call `set` on a list that does not need
   changing, because it may be immutable (exercise 02).
5. **Map choice is a promise about order.** HashMap scrambles,
   LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order, TreeMap sorts (exercises 03, 06).
6. **Lazy means you stop pulling.** Copying an `Iterable` into a list
   before searching reads the whole source (exercise 03).
7. **`andThen` order is "this, then next".** Swapping the calls still
   compiles (exercise 04).
8. **Two interfaces with the same default force an override.** Call a
   specific one with `Greeter.super.greeting()` (exercise 04).
9. **`.reversed()` reverses the whole chain, and the nulls with it.**
   Pass the direction for ONE key: `thenComparing(key, reverseOrder())`,
   `nullsLast(reverseOrder())` (exercise 05).
10. **Long ids sort as numbers only if you keep them as Longs.**
    `"10" < "9"` as strings (exercise 06).
11. **Validate the whole batch before writing any of it** (exercise 06).
12. **Check on write, not only on read.** A raw key puts a bad value in
    the map; it fails much later unless `put` casts (exercise 07).
13. **`int.class.cast(5)` throws.** Type tokens must be wrapper classes
    (exercise 07).
14. **`Optional.of(f(x))` throws on null; `optional.map(f)` drops it**
    (exercise 08).

## Cheat table

| want | write |
| --- | --- |
| largest of anything comparable | `<T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T>)` |
| copy into a wider collection | `<T> void copy(Collection<? super T> dst, Collection<? extends T> src)` |
| explicit type arguments | `Exercise.<Number, Number>zip(ints, doubles)` |
| group into lists | `map.computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new ArrayList<>()).add(v)` |
| sort by key, one key descending | `comparing(A::x).thenComparing(A::y, reverseOrder())` |
| nulls last, descending | `comparing(A::y, nullsLast(reverseOrder()))` |
| call a specific default | `Greeter.super.greeting()` |
| runtime type check | `type.cast(value)` with a `Class<T>` |

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-bounded-max.java` | ★☆☆ | `max`, `clamp` and `topN` with `Comparable<? super T>` |
| 02 | `02-wildcards-pecs.java` | ★☆☆ | copy, sum and range helpers with `? extends` / `? super`, wildcard capture |
| 03 | `03-generic-methods.java` | ★★☆ | `invert`, `zip`, `indexBy` and a lazy `firstMatch` |
| 04 | `04-default-methods.java` | ★★☆ | composable pricing rules on an interface, and the diamond rule |
| 05 | `05-comparator-composition.java` | ★★☆ | multi-key, nulls-last, explicit-order and case-aware comparators |
| 06 | `06-generic-repository.java` | ★★☆ | one `InMemoryRepository<T extends Entity<ID>, ID>` for every entity |
| 07 | `07-typesafe-container.java` | ★★★ | a typed-key context map that a raw type cannot corrupt |
| 08 | `08-functional-pipeline.java` | ★★★ | an immutable `Pipeline<I, O>` of map, filter, flatMap and peek steps |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows. Exercise 06
is the shape behind Spring Data's `CrudRepository<T, ID>`. The keys in
07 are how frameworks store request attributes. The pipeline in 08 is a
small `Stream`, and the next module's `Result<T>` is built the same way.

---

javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.instructions:
**Concepts:** bounded type parameters · Comparable<? super T> · stable sort  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Three generic helpers with the bound T extends Comparable<? super T>,
so they accept Integer, String, and also Beta, which inherits compareTo
from Version. Finish them:

  max(items)        the largest item; on equal maxima, the FIRST one
                    met; an empty collection throws
                    IllegalArgumentException
  clamp(v, lo, hi)  v pinned into [lo, hi], both ends inclusive; lo
                    above hi throws IllegalArgumentException
  topN(items, n)    a new list of the n largest, largest first, equal
                    items in the order met; n above the size gives
                    them all; n < 0 throws IllegalArgumentException

    max(List.of(3, 9, 4))         → 9
    clamp(42, 1, 10)              → 10
    topN(List.of(5, 1, 7, 3), 2)  → [7, 5]

hint: List.sort is stable, and Comparator has a reverseOrder().
javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.explanation:
T extends Comparable<T> is the textbook bound, and it is too strict.
Beta extends Version, so Beta is a Comparable<Version>, not a
Comparable<Beta>: with that bound, `Beta newest = max(betas)` does not
compile, because T would have to be Beta.
T extends Comparable<? super T> reads "T can be compared with some
supertype of itself"; it is exactly what Collections.max declares. The
parameter is Collection<? extends T>, so a List<Beta> can also feed a
call where T is inferred as Version.
max keeps the first of equal maxima because it replaces the best only
on a strictly greater item. Writing ">=" quietly keeps the last one,
and a caller that relies on "first wins" breaks without any error.
topN sorts a COPY with Comparator.reverseOrder(). List.sort is stable,
so equal items keep their encounter order even in descending order.
Sorting the caller's collection in place would be the classic side
effect; copying first is what makes the helper safe to call.

javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.instructions:
**Concepts:** wildcards · PECS · ? extends · ? super · wildcard capture  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

"Producer extends, consumer super": read from a Collection<? extends T>,
write into a Collection<? super T>. Finish five helpers:

  copyAll(dst, src)       add every src item to dst in order; return how
                          many adds dst accepted (a Set may refuse some)
  sum(numbers)            the total of any Numbers as a double; 0.0 if
                          empty
  addRange(sink, a, b)    add the Integers a, a+1, ... b-1 to sink;
                          b < a throws IllegalArgumentException
  copyMatching(src, keep, dst)  like copyAll, only items keep accepts
  swapEnds(list)          swap the first and last item of a List<?>;
                          a list with under 2 items is not touched

    copyAll(List<Number> [1.5], List.of(1, 2))  → 2, dst [1.5, 1, 2]
    addRange(sink, 3, 6)                        → adds 3, 4, 5

hint: you cannot set into a List<?>, but a generic helper can.
javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.explanation:
PECS (Bloch, Effective Java item 31): a parameter you only READ from
is a producer, so it is "? extends T"; one you only WRITE into is a
consumer, so it is "? super T". That is why copyAll can take a
List<Integer> as src and a List<Number> or List<Object> as dst, and
why Collections.copy has exactly this signature.
copyAll returns the number of adds that returned true. Returning
src.size() is the classic wrong turn: a Set refuses duplicates and
the count lies.
sum reads through Number.doubleValue(), the one method every Number
has; it works for Integer, Long, Double and BigDecimal alike.
swapEnds shows WILDCARD CAPTURE. Through a List<?> you can read
Objects but never set anything (the element type is unknown). A
private generic helper swap(List<T>) "captures" the unknown type as T,
and then get/set type-check. The size guard is not just tidiness: it
means an immutable List.of(7) is never written to, so it never throws.

javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.instructions:
**Concepts:** generic methods · type inference · type witness · laziness  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A small generic toolkit for reports. Finish four methods:

  invert(map)        value → keys with that value; the result's values
                     appear in first-seen order, each key list in the
                     map's iteration order
  zip(as, bs)        Pairs of same-index items, stopping at the shorter
  indexBy(items, f)  key → item in encounter order; two items with the
                     same key throw IllegalStateException whose message
                     contains the key
  firstMatch(items, p)  the first item p accepts, or empty; it must
                     stop pulling items from the Iterable once found

    invert({ana=red, bob=blue, cy=red})  → {red=[ana, cy], blue=[bob]}
    zip([1, 2, 3], [a, b])               → [Pair(1, a), Pair(2, b)]
    Exercise.<Number, Number>zip(...)    → explicit type arguments

hint: of HashMap, LinkedHashMap and TreeMap, one keeps insertion order.
javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.explanation:
A generic METHOD declares its own type parameters before the return
type (static <K, V> Map<V, List<K>> invert(...)), so each call can
bind them freely; the compiler infers them from the arguments and the
target type. When inference picks something you did not want, a TYPE
WITNESS states it: Exercise.<Number, Number>zip(ints, doubles). The
parameters are "? extends A" so a List<Integer> can be an A = Number.
invert and indexBy build LinkedHashMaps: a HashMap would scramble the
order of the report, and a TreeMap would sort it, which is a different
promise. computeIfAbsent(v, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(key) is the
idiom for "group into lists".
indexBy refuses duplicates loudly. Map.put would silently keep the last
item, and Collectors.toMap throws only with a message you do not
control; checking put's return value gives a precise error.
firstMatch walks the iterator and returns on the first hit. Copying the
Iterable into a list first, or streaming it all and filtering, pulls
every item: on a database cursor or an infinite source that is a bug,
not a slowdown.

javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.instructions:
**Concepts:** default methods · static interface methods · diamond rule  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A checkout's pricing rules are one-method interfaces that compose.
Finish PricingRule's static factories and default combinators:

  percentOff(p)   price * (100 - p) / 100, rounded HALF_UP to cents;
                  p outside 0..100 throws IllegalArgumentException
  amountOff(a)    price - a, never below 0.00, scale 2
  identity()      returns the price unchanged
  andThen(next)   apply this rule, then next to its result
  floorAt(min)    this rule's result, but never under min
  all(rules)      the rules chained in list order; empty = identity
Then finish Kiosk.greeting(): both interfaces define a default
greeting(), so Kiosk must choose. Return Greeter's, " / ", Localized's.

    percentOff(10).apply(19.99)                     → 17.99
    percentOff(10).andThen(amountOff(5)).apply(100) → 85.00
    amountOff(5).andThen(percentOff(10)).apply(100) → 85.50

hint: inside a default method, `this` is the rule being extended.
javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.explanation:
Since Java 8 an interface can carry behaviour: STATIC methods are
factories that belong to the interface (PricingRule.percentOff(10)
reads better than a PricingRules utility class), and DEFAULT methods
are combinators every implementation inherits for free. Because
PricingRule has one abstract method, each factory just returns a
lambda, and each default wraps `this` in a new lambda. This is the
exact shape of Comparator.thenComparing and Function.andThen.
Order matters in andThen: "this first, then next". Swapping the two
calls compiles and gives 85.50 instead of 85.00 on a 100.00 basket, a
bug that only a test with real numbers notices.
Rounding happens once per rule, HALF_UP to two places, with
divide(HUNDRED, 2, HALF_UP). A bare divide(HUNDRED) keeps every digit
(19.99 * 90 / 100 is 17.991), so the scale would drift rule by rule.
The DIAMOND rule: when two interfaces give the same default, the class
does not compile until it overrides the method. Inside the override,
Greeter.super.greeting() calls a specific interface's version.

javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.instructions:
**Concepts:** Comparator · thenComparing · nullsLast · reversed · stability  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

An HR screen sorts people several ways. Build each Comparator by
composing Comparator's own factories:

  byDeptThenSeniority()      dept A-Z, then level HIGH to low, then
                             name A-Z
  bySalaryNullsLast(desc)    by salary, ascending or descending;
                             a null salary (unknown) is ALWAYS last
  explicitOrder(order)       items in the list's order; items not in
                             the list come after all listed ones and
                             compare equal to each other
  caseInsensitiveThenNatural()  ignore case first; on a tie, natural
                             order (so "Apple" before "apple")
  isSorted(items, cmp)       true if no item compares above the next

    sort [new, zeta, wip] by explicitOrder([new, wip]) → [new, wip, zeta]
    [banana, Apple, apple]  → [Apple, apple, banana]

hint: reversed() reverses everything before it, nulls included.
javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.explanation:
Comparator is built for composition: comparing(key), then
thenComparing(key) for tie-breaks, each optionally with its own
comparator for that key. So "level high to low" is
thenComparing(Employee::level, Comparator.reverseOrder()), which
reverses ONE key. Calling .reversed() on the chain instead reverses
the dept and name order too: the classic composition bug.
The same trap hides in nulls: nullsLast(naturalOrder()).reversed()
moves the nulls to the FRONT, because reversed flips the whole
comparator. Put the direction inside: nullsLast(reverseOrder()).
explicitOrder ranks each item by its index and gives every unlisted
item the same rank (Integer.MAX_VALUE). Because List.sort is a stable
merge sort, equal-rank items keep their original order, which is the
behaviour the tests pin.
String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER.thenComparing(naturalOrder()) is a total
order; case-insensitive alone calls "Apple" and "apple" equal, and a
TreeSet built on it would silently drop one of them.

javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.instructions:
**Concepts:** generic classes · recursive bounds · Entity<ID> · paging  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

One repository class serves Customers (Long ids) and Skus (String
ids). Finish InMemoryRepository. Every list it returns is in id order:
numeric for Long, A-Z for String.

  save(e)          insert or replace; returns the previous row, or
                   empty; a null id throws IllegalArgumentException
  saveAll(es)      all or nothing: if any id is null, throw
                   IllegalArgumentException and save none of them
  findById, findAll, findWhere(p), count()
  deleteById(id)   true if a row was removed
  project(f)       f applied to every row
  page(i, size)    rows i*size .. i*size+size-1 (i from 0); past the
                   end gives []; i < 0 or size < 1 throws
                   IllegalArgumentException

    ids saved as 10, 9, 100   → findAll ids [9, 10, 100]

hint: check every entity before you store the first one.
javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.explanation:
The class signature does the design work:
InMemoryRepository<T extends Entity<ID>, ID extends Comparable<? super
ID>>. "T extends Entity<ID>" ties the row type to its id type, so a
repository of Customers only accepts Long ids in findById; "ID extends
Comparable" is what lets a TreeMap keep the rows sorted by id. One
class, checked for every entity type, with no casts: that is the point
of generics over a repository of Object.
Long ids sort numerically (9 before 10 before 100) only because the
TreeMap compares Longs. Keying by id.toString() would give "10" < "9",
a bug you meet in real code that builds cache keys from strings.
saveAll validates the whole batch before touching the map, which is
the in-memory version of a transaction: half a batch saved is worse
than none, because the caller cannot tell which half.
page computes a window over findAll(). Clamp both ends to the size:
from = min(i * size, n), to = min(from + size, n), so a page past the
end is an empty list rather than an IndexOutOfBoundsException.

javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.instructions:
**Concepts:** typed keys · Class<T>.cast · type tokens · raw types  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

A request context holds values of many types under typed keys, so
ctx.require(PORT) is an Integer with no cast. Finish Key's compact
constructor (a primitive such as int.class throws
IllegalArgumentException) and Context:

  put(key, v)        store v; a null v REMOVES the key; a value that is
                     not really a T (smuggled in through a raw Key)
                     throws ClassCastException and stores nothing
  get(key), getOrDefault(key, f)   the value, or empty / f
  require(key)       the value, or NoSuchElementException whose
                     message contains the key's name
  names()            "name:SimpleTypeName" per stored key, sorted
Keys are equal when name AND type match: ("timeout", Integer) and
("timeout", String) are different keys.

    put(PORT, 8080); require(PORT) → 8080; names() → [port:Integer]

hint: a Class<T> object can check a value as well as name a type.
javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.explanation:
This is Bloch's "typesafe heterogeneous container" (Effective Java
item 33). The map itself is Map<Key<?>, Object>, so the compiler
cannot help inside it; the type safety lives in the KEY. A Key<T>
carries a Class<T> type token, and every read goes through
key.type().cast(value), which returns a T without an unchecked cast.
The same cast on WRITE is what makes the container honest. Generics
are erased at runtime, so a raw Key lets a caller put a String under
an Integer key with only a compiler warning. Without the check the
bad value sits in the map and blows up later, far from the bug, with
a ClassCastException at some innocent call site. Casting in put fails
at the line that caused it. Collections.checkedList does the same.
Primitive keys are refused because int.class.cast(8080) throws: the
value is boxed to Integer, and Integer is not an int. The type token
must be the wrapper class.
Records give Key a correct equals/hashCode for free, and because the
type takes part in equality, one name can hold two typed values.

javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.instructions:
**Concepts:** Function composition · Optional · immutability · wildcards  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

An import job cleans each raw line through a chain of steps. Build
Pipeline<I, O>: input type I, current output type O. It wraps a
Function<I, Optional<O>>; an empty Optional means "dropped". Finish:

  start()        a Pipeline<T, T> passing input through; null → empty
  map(f)         transform; if f returns null the item is dropped
  filter(p)      drop items p rejects
  flatMap(f)     f returns an Optional; empty drops the item
  peek(action)   run action on each item that REACHES this step
  then(next)     run another pipeline on what survives this one
  run(input)     the Optional result for one input
  runAll(inputs) the survivors' results, in input order

A dropped item never reaches later steps, and every step returns a NEW
pipeline: the one you called it on is unchanged.
    start().map(String::trim).map(Integer::parseInt).run(" 42 ") → 42

hint: Optional already has map, filter and flatMap with these rules.
javabootcamp/14-generics-and-interfaces/.explanation:
The pipeline is a function I -> Optional<O>, and each step returns a
new Pipeline wrapping a bigger function: map(f) is
in -> run.apply(in).map(f). Nothing runs until run(...) is called;
building the chain only composes functions. Because the field is final
and every step builds a new object, a shared prefix can be branched
safely: base.map(a) and base.map(b) never see each other.
Optional carries the "dropped" rule for free. Optional.map turns a null
result into empty, filter empties on a rejection, and once a value is
empty, map/filter/flatMap/ifPresent skip their function. That is why a
peek after a filter never sees dropped items, with no if-statement
anywhere. Optional.of(f.apply(x)) in map is the classic slip: it
throws NullPointerException instead of dropping.
The wildcards are what make the steps reusable: map takes a
Function<? super O, ? extends R>, so a Function<Object, String> or a
method returning a subtype both fit. then(Pipeline<? super O, ?
extends R>) lets a validation pipeline written for a supertype run
after this one.
